h1:
Nong Khai–Udon Thani 3 Days
Mekong, Udon City & the Red Lotus Sea
intro: Nong Khai and Udon Thani sit only about 53 km apart, with trains running between them in under an hour, so they pair up neatly into a single trip. This plan runs 3 days: start slow and quiet along the Mekong in Nong Khai, pay respects to Luang Pho Phra Sai, eat naem nueang, then move down to the busier city of Udon. The real highlight comes last — an early-morning boat ride across the Red Lotus Sea at Nong Han Kumphawapi, a field of pink lotus blooming out on the water that only peaks in the cool season. We've packed in the opening hours, boat fares and the spots locals actually go to.

blocks.html: First, the lay of the land. Nong Khai sits right on the Lao border — a small town with a slow pace, its appeal centered on the Mekong River. Udon Thani is about 53 km further south, a regional hub that's bigger and more lively, with an international airport. Plenty of people fly into Udon and fan out from there. So this trip runs north to south: start in Nong Khai, then drift down to Udon, leaving the last day close to the airport for an easy ride home. The Red Lotus Sea is in Kumphawapi district, another 40 km or so south of Udon city — and you'll want an early start, since the lotus close up by mid-morning.

blocks.text: When the Red Lotus Sea blooms, and how to plan around it

blocks.html: Let's be straight about this before you plan: the Red Lotus Sea doesn't bloom year-round. The lotus start opening in the late-rains, early-cool stretch around November and last until roughly late February or early March, with the fullest bloom in December and January. Come outside that window and Nong Han is just an open sheet of water with no flowers to see. That's why this trip suits the cool season best — while Nong Khai and Udon city are fine to visit any time of year.

blocks.title: An early start is everything
blocks.html: The red lotus only open fully in the morning, then gradually close as the sun gets stronger. Boats run from around 6:00, and the prettiest window is 6:00–9:00. Arrive much past 10–11 a.m. and a lot of the flowers will already have closed, so it's worth basing your last night near Kumphawapi or setting off before dawn from Udon city.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Nong Khai: the Mekong and Tha Sadet Market

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Start along the Mekong in Nong Khai

items.activity: Arrive in Nong Khai, check in to a place in town
items.note: If you fly into Udon, hop a minivan or train up to Nong Khai first, around 1 hr. Pick a place near the Mekong or close to Tha Sadet Market so you can wander out easily at night.

items.activity: Lunch at Daeng Naem Nueang, a Vietnamese spot
items.note: A long-running, well-known Vietnamese restaurant in Nong Khai. The naem nueang is charcoal-grilled and made fresh daily, wrapped in rice paper with fresh herbs. Add the sugarcane shrimp and fried spring rolls.

items.activity: Pay respects to Luang Pho Phra Sai at Wat Pho Chai
items.note: A roughly 300-year-old temple that's central to the town. Luang Pho Phra Sai is a revered Buddha image honored by Thais and Lao alike — dress modestly.

items.activity: Break at an old-building cafe in the town center
items.note: Nong Khai has cafes in colonial buildings nearly a century old, with a feel a bit like Luang Prabang. Sip a coffee out of the afternoon sun before heading to the riverside.

items.activity: Stroll the Naga Plaza along the Mekong
items.note: The town's landmark — a pair of nagas in front of Wat Lamduan, next to Tha Sadet Market. Locals come here to walk, cycle and exercise in the evening.

items.activity: Watch the sunset over the Lao side
items.note: The golden hour over the Mekong is the highlight of the day. Find a spot on the bank or a riverside restaurant, order something and wait for the evening light.

items.activity: Eat your way through Tha Sadet Market
items.note: An old riverside market with plenty of snacks. Try the pâté baguette (French bread filled with liver pâté and mu yo pork sausage) and the dried-goods souvenirs from Laos.

items.activity: Dinner at a riverside Mekong-fish restaurant, then back to your room
items.note: Pick a freshwater-fish spot or an Isan place by the river. End the day in the cool breeze, then walk back to your room.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Temples in Nong Khai, then shift your base down to Udon

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Nong Khai in the morning, Udon in the afternoon

items.activity: Nong Khai-style breakfast
items.note: Rice-noodle congee (khao piak sen), old-school coffee and sangkhaya custard toast — a border-town breakfast that's easy to find around town.

items.activity: Visit Sala Kaew Ku (the sculpture park)
items.note: A park of more than 200 concrete deity statues spread over about 42 rai, around 3 km from town. An offbeat sight you won't easily find elsewhere. Entry for Thais is around 20 THB; open roughly 8:00–18:00.

items.activity: Photograph the First Thai–Lao Friendship Bridge
items.note: A Mekong crossing over 1,170 m long, linking Nong Khai with Vientiane. A pretty riverside photo spot, near Nong Khai train station.

items.activity: Pick up souvenirs at Tha Sadet Market
items.note: Grab mu yo, naem and Chinese sausage, plus dried goods from Laos, before heading down to Udon.

items.activity: Take the train or minivan to Udon Thani
items.note: The train takes about 40 min and tickets start in the low hundreds of baht. Minivans leave every hour, with fares from around 60 THB. The distance is about 53 km.

items.activity: Check in to a place in central Udon
items.note: Choose a central neighborhood near Nong Prajak Park or UD Town so you can walk to food and nightlife easily.

items.activity: Stroll Nong Prajak Silpakhom Public Park
items.note: A city park ringing a large pond, with a giant yellow rubber duck as its landmark. Udon locals come here for evening exercise, and there are cafes along the park.

items.activity: Dinner at VT Naem Nueang
items.note: Udon's famous original Vietnamese restaurant; its Pho Si branch has earned a Bib Gourmand in the Michelin Guide. Soft pork naem nueang with a generous spread of fresh herbs — add some mu yo and crunchy tendon.

items.activity: Wander UD Town night market
items.note: A food-and-drink plaza in the center of town next to Udon train station, with restaurants, snacks and often live music. A good walk to wind down before heading back.

blocks.title: Getting between Nong Khai and Udon
blocks.html: If you're not renting a car, the smoothest option is the train — only about 40 min between Nong Khai and Udon Thani stations. But departures are limited, so check the State Railway schedule (railway.co.th) ahead of time. Minivans run more frequently but depend on traffic. A private car is the most flexible, especially for the last day when you need to reach the Red Lotus Sea before dawn.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Red Lotus Sea at dawn, then a last look at Udon before you go

items.activity: Leave Udon city for Kumphawapi
items.note: The Red Lotus Sea is at Nong Han lake in Kumphawapi district, about 40 km from town — roughly a 45 min to 1 hr drive. Set off before dawn to catch the lotus in bloom.

items.activity: Take a boat across the Red Lotus Sea
items.note: Boats run from around 6:00. A small boat for 2–3 people is about 150 THB/person; a large one for 6–10 people is about 600 THB/boat. The ride lasts about 1 hr. The main pier is Ban Diam, with others at Ban Chiang Wae, Ban Chae Lae and Ban Don Khong Soem.

items.activity: Photos by the pier, breakfast around Kumphawapi
items.note: It's still early after the boat ride, so find a breakfast spot or coffee near the pier and rest before heading back.

items.activity: Back to Udon, stop at the Udon Thani Museum
items.note: An old yellow colonial building in the center of town telling the city's history. Free entry, open Tuesday–Sunday, closed Mondays.

items.activity: Lunch — Isan or fusion food in town
items.note: Udon has plenty of punchy Isan spots — som tam, larb, koi, grilled pork neck. Take your pick before packing up.

items.activity: Souvenir shopping, then to the airport or station
items.note: Grab some naem nueang, mu yo and other Udon souvenirs, then head to Udon Thani Airport or the train station for your trip home.

blocks.title: If you have a Day 4 or want a change of scene
blocks.html: If you finish the Red Lotus Sea early and still have energy, you can continue to Kham Chanot (the Kham Chanot forest, Ban Dung district), a sacred site tied to naga legend, open roughly 6:00–18:00. Or head to the Ban Chiang Museum in Nong Han district, a prehistoric archaeological site, open roughly 9:00–16:00. But the two sit in different directions and are fairly far apart — you'll want a car and some buffer time.

blocks.text: Food from both provinces worth trying on this trip

blocks.html: Both Nong Khai and Udon blend Isan and Vietnamese culture, so the food overlaps in places but each has its own standouts. Here are the dishes and spots locals actually go to, in the order we'd try them on a two-province trip like this.

items.name: VT Naem Nueang — Udon Thani
items.blurb: Udon's most famous original Vietnamese restaurant; the Pho Si branch has earned a Bib Gourmand from the Michelin Guide. Soft pork naem nueang, nicely grilled and fragrant, served with a generous spread of fresh herbs — pair it with mu yo and crunchy tendon.

items.name: Daeng Naem Nueang — Nong Khai
items.blurb: The famous name on the Nong Khai side, with naem nueang made fresh daily and grilled on skewers over charcoal the old-fashioned way. Most people passing through Nong Khai stop here — try it against VT and see which you prefer.

items.name: Mekong river fish — riverside spots in Nong Khai
items.blurb: A Mekong town calls for freshwater fish — tom yum, fish larb, or fried with chili sauce, the flesh fresh from the river. It goes even better with a river view at dusk.

items.name: Isan food in Udon
items.blurb: Udon is the real deal for bold Isan flavors — som tam, larb, koi, grilled pork neck, all big on taste and easy to find across town. Eat it with cold sticky rice.

items.name: Pâté baguette — Tha Sadet Market
items.blurb: A baguette crisp outside and soft inside, filled with liver pâté and mu yo sausage — a Vietnamese influence that makes for a fun snack while you wander the riverside market.

items.name: Sugarcane shrimp
items.blurb: Minced shrimp wrapped around a sugarcane stick and grilled, faintly sweet and fragrant. Usually ordered alongside naem nueang at the Vietnamese spots in both Nong Khai and Udon.

items.name: Cafes by Nong Prajak Park
items.blurb: The area around Nong Prajak Park has several cafes. Sip a coffee or matcha looking out over the pond and the yellow rubber duck — a good evening break.

items.name: Coffee in an old building, central Nong Khai
items.blurb: A cafe in a colonial building nearly a century old, with a feel a bit like Luang Prabang. A good place to rest out of the afternoon sun between riverside walks.

items.name: Fried spring rolls
items.blurb: Tightly packed spring rolls fried crisp, dipped in a sweet-and-sour sauce — a popular snack at the Vietnamese restaurants in both towns.

items.name: Mu yo and naem — souvenirs from both towns
items.blurb: The souvenirs worth carrying home: dense mu yo pork sausage and nicely tangy naem. You can find them at Tha Sadet Market in Nong Khai and at souvenir shops in Udon.

blocks.text: The main sights in this two-province plan

items.name: Red Lotus Sea, Nong Han Kumphawapi
items.blurb: A broad lake where red-pink lotus bloom across the whole surface in the cool season. Take a boat at dawn — the highlight of this trip.

items.name: Naga Plaza on the Mekong, Nong Khai
items.blurb: The town's landmark — a pair of nagas in front of Wat Lamduan, beside Tha Sadet Market. Catch the cool breeze and watch the sun set over the Lao side.

items.name: Sala Kaew Ku (sculpture park)
items.blurb: A park of more than 200 concrete deity statues over about 42 rai, an offbeat sight about 3 km from Nong Khai town.

items.name: Wat Pho Chai (Luang Pho Phra Sai)
items.blurb: A roughly 300-year-old temple central to Nong Khai, home to Luang Pho Phra Sai, a revered Buddha image for people on both banks of the Mekong.

items.name: Nong Prajak Silpakhom Public Park
items.blurb: A park around a large pond in central Udon, with a giant yellow rubber duck as its landmark — a favorite local spot to relax.

items.name: Udon Thani Museum
items.blurb: An old yellow colonial building in the center of town telling Udon's history. Free entry, closed Mondays.

blocks.text: How to get around and plan a smooth trip

items: Trip direction — start in Nong Khai, then drift down to Udon, since the last day takes you to the Red Lotus Sea south of Udon and lets you finish right by Udon airport.
Between the two towns — the Nong Khai–Udon train takes about 40 min, or minivans leave every hour from around 60 THB. The distance is roughly 53 km.
Within Nong Khai town — the riverside, Naga Plaza and Tha Sadet Market are all walkable, while Sala Kaew Ku is a little outside town, so a car helps.
Getting to the Red Lotus Sea — it's in Kumphawapi, about 40 km from Udon city. A private car or chartered ride is best, since you need to leave before dawn before the lotus close.
Crossing to Vientiane — with an extra day, you can cross the border at the Friendship Bridge to see the Lao side. Have your passport ready.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: The two towns charm you in different ways. Nong Khai is slow and quiet, all about the Mekong atmosphere, while Udon is lively in a big-city way, with more food and cafes to choose from. Come in the wrong season and the Red Lotus Sea is just open water, so if the lotus field is what you're after, aim squarely for the cool season (Nov–Feb).

items: 2 nights' lodging — first night on the Mekong in Nong Khai, second in Udon city. Hotels/guesthouses start around ฿500–1,500 per night.
Food — main meals at Vietnamese/Isan spots run about ฿150–300 each, plus market snacks and cafes.
Red Lotus Sea boat — a small boat is about ฿150 per person, or a large boat about ฿600 per boat (split it if you're a group).
Entry fees — Sala Kaew Ku is ฿20; most everything else is free (temples, parks, the Udon museum, Naga Plaza).
Travel between towns — train/minivan in the tens to low hundreds of baht, plus a chartered ride to the Red Lotus Sea before dawn.
Total per person — at an easy, unfussy pace, around ฿2,500–4,000 per person (not including airfare into the province).

faq.q: Can you visit both Nong Khai and Udon Thani in one trip?
faq.a: Easily. The two provinces are only about 53 km apart, with trains running between them in around 40 min, or minivans every hour. A nice plan is one night by the Mekong in Nong Khai, then a move down to Udon for another night, finishing with the Red Lotus Sea on the morning of the last day before flying out of Udon.

faq.q: When does the Red Lotus Sea bloom, and when should I go?
faq.a: The red lotus bloom in the late-rains, early-cool stretch from around November to late February or early March, with the fullest bloom in December and January. They only open fully in the morning before the sun gets strong, so take a boat between 6:00 and 9:00. Go out of season and you'll see only water, no flowers.

faq.q: How much is a Red Lotus Sea boat, and what are the hours?
faq.a: Boats start running around 6:00 and continue until about 17:00. A small boat for 2–3 people is about 150 THB per person; a large boat for 6–10 people is about 600 THB per boat. The ride lasts about an hour. The main pier is Ban Diam in Kumphawapi district, around 40 km from Udon city.

faq.q: What's the easiest way to travel between Nong Khai and Udon Thani?
faq.a: If you don't have a car, the smoothest option is the train — about 40 min between Nong Khai and Udon Thani stations — but departures are limited, so check the railway schedule ahead. Minivans run more often, with fares from around 60 THB. A private car is the most flexible, especially on the day you head to the Red Lotus Sea before dawn.

faq.q: What food should I try on a Nong Khai–Udon trip?
faq.a: The standout is naem nueang, and each town has its own famous name — VT Naem Nueang on the Udon side, Daeng Naem Nueang on the Nong Khai side. After that, riverside Mekong fish in Nong Khai, bold Isan food in Udon, the pâté baguette at Tha Sadet Market, and souvenirs like mu yo and naem.
